canonical.title: Stable, rolling, or atomic: picking a release model for your first Linux daily driver

parent.title: Which Linux to switch to in 2026: a decision framework for a .NET developer leaving Windows

siblings.title: The 2026 Linux distro landscape: what actually differs between the families
siblings.summary: There are only five real distro families, and for a Windows developer moving to Linux in 2026 the honest shortlist is Fedora Workstation, Ubuntu LTS, Linux Mint, Bluefin/Aurora, and openSUSE Tumbleweed — everything else is a variation, a server OS, or a hobby.

siblings.title: Toolchain fit: which Linux distro costs least setup work for .NET 10 + TypeScript + Docker in 2026
siblings.summary: For a .NET 10 + TypeScript + Docker workstation in 2026, Ubuntu 26.04 LTS and Fedora 44 tie on setup effort and every other family costs you at least one hand-configured vendor repo.

siblings.title: Picking a Linux desktop in 2026: the Windows 11 switcher's decision guide
siblings.summary: KDE Plasma is the lowest-friction landing spot for a Windows 11 developer in 2026; X11 sessions die this year, so the real choice is which Wayland compositor's rough edges you can live with.

siblings.title: Hardware and driver reality in 2026: only three things should decide your distro
siblings.summary: In 2026 only three hardware classes still force a distro choice — NVIDIA, very new silicon, and Secure-Boot dual-boot; everything else is a live-USB check away.

siblings.title: Windows to Linux in 2026: what crosses over, what doesn't, and how to stage the switch
siblings.summary: Almost everything a .NET developer does crosses to Linux in 2026 — the four things that don't are desktop Office with VBA, a native Outlook with working calendar, WPF/WinForms designers, and Windows-only compliance tooling.

siblings.title: Linux upkeep in 2026: support windows, upgrade pain, and monthly chores ranked
siblings.summary: Ranked by ongoing upkeep for a learning-level Linux user: atomic Fedora and Ubuntu/Mint LTS are near-zero chore; Fedora Workstation costs one upgrade a year; Arch costs a reading habit you cannot skip.

siblings.title: Gaming and media on Linux in 2026: singleplayer is solved, anti-cheat and DRM streaming are not
siblings.summary: Roughly 90% of Windows Steam titles launch under Proton; the two real losses are kernel anti-cheat multiplayer and browser DRM streaming above 720p SDR.

sources.title: Fedora 44 release date confirmed (OSTechNix)
sources.claim: Fedora 44 was released on 28 April 2026, continuing Fedora's roughly six-month release cadence.

sources.title: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS release notes
sources.claim: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS was released 23 April 2026 with five years of security updates through April 2031.

sources.title: Fedora 44 with btrfs snapshot and rollback support (SysGuides)
sources.claim: Fedora's default installer does not create a btrfs layout suited to snapshot management, and automatic pre/post snapshots require manually installing snapper plus the DNF5 actions plugin and grub-btrfs.

sources.title: Bluefin administration guide
sources.claim: Bluefin checks for updates every six hours and applies them at reboot; the stable stream publishes weekly images with a kernel gated about two weeks behind Fedora; rollback uses bootc status / bootc switch to dated tags; local package layering is locked off by default.

sources.title: Arch Linux news feed
sources.claim: Arch Linux posted roughly thirteen manual-intervention or breaking-change advisories between January 2025 and July 2026, plus an active malicious-AUR-package incident in June 2026.

sources.title: Debian trixie package: nodejs
sources.claim: Debian 13 trixie ships nodejs 20.19.2.

sources.title: Node.js previous releases and EOL schedule
sources.claim: Node.js 20 (Iron) reached end-of-life on 24 March 2026; the maintained LTS lines in mid-2026 are 22 and 24, with 26 as Current.

sources.title: Debian 13 trixie release notes — what's new
sources.claim: Debian 13 trixie ships the Linux 6.12 series, GCC 14.2, Python 3.13, GNOME 48 and KDE Plasma 6.3.6.

sources.title: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS now available, powered by Linux 7.0 (Phoronix)
sources.claim: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS ships the Linux 7.0 kernel for the latest hardware support.

sources.title: openSUSE Snapper documentation
sources.claim: openSUSE integrates snapper with btrfs as a first-class, default-enabled helper for reverting the system to a previous state.

sources.title: rpm-ostree administrator handbook
sources.claim: Every rpm-ostree operation is offline and composes a new deployment applied at reboot; the system keeps two bootable deployments and rpm-ostree rollback swaps the default; most software should go into a container.

sources.title: Can't update Fedora Kinoite 44, probably NVIDIA related (Fedora Discussion)
sources.claim: A May 2026 Fedora Kinoite 44 thread shows an update blocked by an NVIDIA akmod dependency conflict during a kernel bump.

sources.title: openSUSE Tumbleweed: updating, upgrading and reverting
sources.claim: openSUSE Tumbleweed publishes snapshots several times a week, gated by openQA testing; the update command is zypper dup, and rollback is done by booting a read-only snapshot from GRUB2 then running snapper rollback.

sources.title: Fedora 43→44 upgrade keeps failing and rolling back (Fedora Discussion)
sources.claim: In June 2026 the Fedora 43 to 44 upgrade silently failed on btrfs-subvolume layouts because the /system-update symlink was invisible to systemd; the workaround was dropping to a non-graphical target and using dnf-3 instead of dnf5.

sources.title: Updated Debian 13: 13.6 released
sources.claim: Debian 13.6 was released on 11 July 2026 as a point release of the trixie stable series.

sources.title: Fedora release life cycle
sources.claim: Each Fedora release is supported for about 13 months — until roughly one month after the release of version X+2 — allowing users to skip a release.

sources.title: Leap 16 doubles support (openSUSE News)
sources.claim: From Leap 16.0 onward every minor release receives 24 months of maintenance, enabled by sharing a binary core with SUSE Linux Enterprise.

sources.title: Leap 15 reaches end of life (openSUSE News)
sources.claim: openSUSE Leap 15 reached end of life in April 2026, closing a roughly eight-year era.

sources.title: openSUSE Aeon review (LWN)
sources.claim: openSUSE Aeon targets 'lazy developers' with automated snapshot-based updates applied at reboot and automatic updates of the OS, Flatpaks and distroboxes, but ships almost no base software and is explicitly not for system tinkerers.

sources.title: Arch Wiki: pacman package signing
sources.claim: Arch upgrades can fail on a stale signing keyring after long gaps; the fix is pacman -Sy --needed archlinux-keyring before pacman -Su, and a weekly systemd timer refreshes trusted key signatures.

sources.title: pacman errors when updating Arch after a long time
sources.claim: Machines left un-updated for a long period hit interrupted pacman upgrades caused by out-of-date keyring packages.

sources.title: NixOS manual
sources.claim: NixOS is configured declaratively and every configuration change adds a boot-menu entry (a generation) that can be booted to roll back.

sources.title: NixOS Wiki: nixos-rebuild
sources.claim: nixos-rebuild creates new system generations; rolling back means selecting an older generation in the boot menu.

sources.title: Install and use Timeshift on Fedora (FOSS Linux)
sources.claim: Timeshift's btrfs mode only supports Ubuntu-style @ and @home subvolume layouts, so Fedora users are steered to the slower rsync mode.

sources.title: dotnet/sdk issue 48973 — libicu76 on Debian trixie
sources.claim: Microsoft's official .NET packages failed to install on Debian trixie because their metadata declared libicu52 through libicu74 while trixie ships libicu76.

sources.title: HWE kernels on Ubuntu LTS (OneUptime)
sources.claim: Ubuntu LTS releases freeze their kernel at release time, so hardware bought later may lack drivers; HWE kernels backport newer upstream kernels into the LTS.

sources.title: Ubuntu kernel lifecycle
sources.claim: Ubuntu LTS offers a GA kernel frozen at release and an HWE stack that provides newer kernel and display support on a rolling basis, with desktop installs defaulting to HWE.

sources.title: Ubuntu virtualization HWE stack (Phoronix)
sources.claim: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS adds a virtualization HWE stack shipping newer QEMU, libvirt, EDK2 and SeaBIOS via -hwe packages, refreshed every six months during the first two years of the LTS.

sources.title: Bazzite, SteamOS and Linux gaming at 3.2% (Tech Insider)
sources.claim: Bazzite, a Fedora Atomic based image, reached about 5.53% share among Linux Steam users in late 2025 while Linux overall hit an all-time-high 3.2% of Steam users in 2026.

sources.title: Distrobox, Toolbx, Podman, Docker (falcao.org)
sources.claim: Toolbx is the Red Hat project preinstalled on Fedora Atomic desktops; Distrobox is the community superset that will run any container image as a dev environment.

sources.title: Toolbox, IDEs and atomic desktops (r0x0d)
sources.claim: Using IDEs inside toolbox/distrobox on atomic desktops creates friction at the container boundary — for example needing workarounds to launch a host browser for VS Code's GitHub sign-in.

sources.title: Using Podman on Fedora Silverblue (OneUptime)
sources.claim: Fedora Silverblue preinstalls Podman rather than Docker, and dnf cannot be used to install packages directly on the host.

sources.title: Bluefin DX developer experience (bluefin-docs wiki)
sources.claim: Bluefin DX bakes Docker Engine, Podman, Incus, KVM/QEMU with virt-manager, VS Code with the Remote-Containers extension and Homebrew into the image, activated with ujust devmode plus ujust dx-group.

sources.title: Bluefin documentation home
sources.claim: Bluefin positions itself as not a distribution, with the user's relationship being with Flathub, Homebrew and their own containers rather than a host package manager.

sources.title: Flathub sees over 435 million downloads in 2025 (Linuxiac)
sources.claim: Flathub recorded more than 435 million downloads in 2025, a 21% year-over-year increase and over fifteen times its 2020 volume, across more than 2,800 apps.

sources.title: CachyOS topped DistroWatch rankings (Linuxiac)
sources.claim: CachyOS, an Arch-based rolling release, took the number one DistroWatch position in mid-2025 and held it for over eighteen consecutive months.

sources.title: CachyOS (Wikipedia)
sources.claim: CachyOS is an Arch Linux based rolling-release distribution focused on performance tuning, with a graphical installer and a Handheld Edition.
